subject: english-language
title: The Social Scaffold
welcome_lead: Beyond reinforcement and innateness — Bruner and Vygotsky bring caregivers into the spotlight. Acquisition is collaboration.
meta_desc: Bruner's LASS, Vygotsky's ZPD and social interactionist theories of child language acquisition at A-Level.
final_note: You have seen acquisition as a joint enterprise — caregiver and child building grammar together.

concepts.def: Jerome Bruner proposed a Language Acquisition Support System — the structured caregiver interaction (peekaboo, joint attention) that scaffolds language.
Adult speech to children featuring exaggerated intonation, simplified vocabulary and frequent repetition — also called motherese.
Lev Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development — the gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with guidance.
Theory (Bruner, Vygotsky) that language emerges from meaningful interaction with caregivers, balancing innateness and learning.
Shared focus between caregiver and child on an object or event — a precursor to reference and naming.
Bruner's metaphor for the temporary support caregivers provide that is gradually withdrawn as the child becomes competent.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Bruner observed that games like peekaboo teach turn-taking, anticipation and joint attention long before words appear.

The LASS provides a predictable structure within which the child learns how dialogue works — slots, roles and reciprocity.

Caregivers across cultures use raised pitch, slowed tempo and exaggerated intonation when speaking to infants. CDS highlights word boundaries and emotional valence.

Far from useless baby talk, CDS is finely tuned to the child's attention and processing capacity.

Vygotsky's ZPD frames learning as social. A child who can name a cat alone but only describe its colour with prompting is in the ZPD for colour vocabulary.

Effective caregivers operate just above the child's solo competence — pulling them upward through guided interaction.
